review_basis: Visually inspected all sixteen original numbered WebP slides directly from GitHub, following actual layout, graphs, flows, labels and worked examples. Topic-first scenes use verified source order.
part_title: Generative AI Limitations, Hallucinations and Content Integrity

scenes.title: Generative AI Capabilities and Limitations
scenes.narration: The left side identifies the strengths of generative AI: adaptability to tasks, creativity, personalization and scale. The right side lists limitations: toxic outputs, hallucinations, privacy exposure, different outputs from the same prompt, plagiarism concerns and difficulty explaining some results. In between, follow the workflow from a clear prompt to a generated draft, review and checks, then a human publication decision. The customer-support example at the bottom shows why this matters. A model can draft a polite message about a delayed order but invent a delivery estimate that no system has verified. The reviewer must check real order details and privacy requirements before publication. A fluent sentence can still be wrong, so fast generation is not the same as trustworthy final content.

scenes.title: Toxicity
scenes.narration: The diagram begins with a user asking for a social-media post. The model generates text, then a guardrail or content filter assesses the draft against the organization's safety policy. Human review handles difficult or ambiguous cases. Toxicity can include offensive, harmful or inappropriate language, but context, quotations and intent affect interpretation. In the lower-left example, a potentially toxic output is flagged and blocked. The lower-right example involves offensive words quoted in news coverage; the text may require human review rather than an automatic decision that the author endorses the language. Safety filtering should reduce harmful outputs while maintaining a process for nuance and false positives. On the exam, recognize guardrails and human review as complementary controls, not infallible automated judgments.

scenes.title: Hallucinations
scenes.narration: A hallucination is a plausible-sounding claim that is unsupported or incorrect. Follow the upper workflow: someone asks about Amazon S3, the system retrieves relevant trusted documentation, the model drafts an answer with citations, and a person or independent check verifies important claims. This retrieval-grounded approach is often called RAG, or retrieval-augmented generation. It reduces risk but cannot guarantee accuracy. The red lower example falsely claims that every S3 object is encrypted with a customer-managed key by default. The green example correctly distinguishes server-side encryption options such as SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS. The important lesson is not just to display a citation; open the cited material and check whether the actual claim follows from it. For high-impact answers, verify facts and applicable configurations before acting.

scenes.title: Plagiarism and Cheating
scenes.narration: Read the four stages in order. AI can help a student brainstorm or draft an outline. The user then verifies facts and traces sources, adds meaningful original analysis and finally submits work with attribution according to the applicable rules. The lower example uses an essay about sustainable cities: generated suggestions are starting material, but the student checks references and contributes their own conclusions. Plagiarism involves using someone else's work without appropriate attribution, while cheating depends on the rules of an assessment or organization. An AI-generated passage can create integrity risks even when it sounds original, and automated AI detectors are not definitive evidence. The appropriate exam response emphasizes source verification, transparent attribution, responsible assistance and meaningful human contribution.
